name: SynapTech ReadRoom Social Cue Enhancer
body_location: cranial — dual micro-processor nodes at the bilateral temporal lobes, with retinal sensor integration
description:
The ReadRoom is a dual-node cranial implant that augments the brain's social cognition circuitry by processing high-resolution visual data from the user's existing retinal feed — or from SynapTech's optional companion retinal layer — and running it through a real-time behavioral inference engine. The system tracks 84 facial muscle movement signatures, gaze direction and duration, postural microshifts, proxemic changes, and respiratory rate visible in neck and chest movement, cross-referencing these against a continuously updated behavioral database to generate a low-latency inference overlay. This overlay is delivered not as an intrusive AR display but as a subtle amplification of the user's own intuition: a mild neural signal that makes a person's discomfort feel more obvious, their enthusiasm more legible, their deception more apparent. Users describe it less as seeing new information and more as finally being able to trust what they were already sensing. For users who opt into the full AR annotation mode, a soft highlight and text tag can appear at the periphery of vision, but this mode is considered intrusive by most experienced users and is typically disabled after the first month.

The ReadRoom was developed explicitly in partnership with neurodivergent advocacy groups and is marketed broadly as an assistive social cognition tool, though its user base has long since expanded far beyond that origin. It is popular with anyone who spends significant time in high-stakes social environments: mediators, social workers, teachers, sales staff, and — though the marketing materials are careful about this — people who simply find social interaction exhausting and want the cognitive load reduced. For neurodivergent users, particularly those with autism spectrum conditions, ADHD, or processing differences that affect social reading, the implant is frequently described as life-changing — not because it makes them neurotypical, but because it gives them access to information that neurotypical people receive automatically. The ReadRoom does not tell you what to do with what it shows you. It just makes sure you see it.
legality: Licensed — requires neurocognitive baseline assessment prior to installation
installation_requirements: Licensed neurotechnology clinic; requires pre-installation cognitive baseline assessment; general local anesthetic; 90-minute procedure; 3-week neural calibration period
maintenance: Quarterly firmware updates via clinic or certified home uplink; annual calibration check recommended; behavioral database updates delivered automatically over mesh

side_effects: Calibration period often includes social overstimulation — crowded spaces feel intensely information-rich until the system learns to filter
Some users report difficulty turning off the inference layer in intimate settings, leading to a sense of clinical distance from people they care about
Mild temporal headaches during the first two weeks as the neural amplification pathways establish
Rare: users who disable the system after extended use report a period of social 'flatness' — ordinary social reading feels dulled for several weeks
cultural_context: The ReadRoom occupies a complex social position in GLMZ. In neurodivergent communities, it carries almost no stigma — it is spoken of in the same register as a hearing implant or a focus regulator, a tool that helps a person access the world more fully. In neurotypical communities, attitudes are more mixed. Some people find the idea that someone is running behavioral inference on them during conversation unsettling — there is a persistent social anxiety, especially in Tier 3 and 4 spaces, about being 'read' without consent. A small etiquette norm has emerged in certain social circles of disclosing ReadRoom use at the start of a sensitive conversation, the way someone might mention they're recording. In professional contexts, it is generally accepted without comment. The Licensed requirement — unusual for lifestyle cyberware — stems from early research suggesting that people with certain acute trauma histories can experience adverse reactions to the overstimulation of the calibration period, requiring clinical screening first.
known_users: Neurodivergent individuals — particularly those with autism spectrum conditions, ADHD, or social processing differences
People managing social anxiety who find the reduced cognitive load helpful
Journalists and investigators who work in high-stakes interview environments
story_hooks: A player character with a ReadRoom notices during a seemingly routine negotiation that every person on the other side of the table is displaying synchronized stress markers — as if they have all been coached, or are all afraid of the same thing.

The party needs to identify which member of a social gathering is lying about their identity — a character with a ReadRoom can attempt to narrow it down, but the target also has a ReadRoom and knows exactly how to perform calm.

A teenager has had a ReadRoom installed by well-meaning parents and is now experiencing severe social withdrawal — they can see too much, and being around people has become overwhelming rather than easier. Someone needs to find them a specialist who can recalibrate the sensitivity threshold.
